foreignObject.h5:div: If the term is unfamiliar to you, here is the short
version: System 1 is the fast, intuitive, and emotional
system, while System 2 is the slow, deliberate, and
logical one. Daniel Kahneman, Nobel Prize laureate
in Economics, coined this term in his psychology
work on judgment and decision making, which
challenged the idea that humans are rational
TypeSafe leaned into this and named their new type
contrast to text-generating Large Language Models
(LLMs), which are more like System 2. Jev is their
How do they compare to LLMs?
LLMs work by predicting the most probable next
token, step by step. Especially for machine-to-
machine communication, people have tried to
squeeze LLM output into a schema. There are
techniques for that, but they limit the model in its
, and they are nowhere near efficient enough
for realtime applications at a feasible cost.
So what does Jev do differently? It takes the same
input as basic LLMs (which is plain text) and a set of
questions with their answer candidates. Its output is
then a set of probabilities for each question. The
model fundamentally does not generate text and
therefore cannot return an answer outside the
mean it cannot pick an incorrect
That reliability and efficiency make it a good fit
Oh, and they are really really cheap. Jev is currently
listed at 0.0047€ per 1M input tokens, with output
tokens being free. TypeSafe attributes this price to
the massive parallelism of its decision heads.
Despite Jev having been released only on September
15th, open-weight alternatives have sprouted up like
mushrooms. They mostly work by architecturally
modifying and fine-tuning a pre-trained language
model on a specific dataset. Since the problem
space is less fragmented, way smaller models get
TypeSafe AI claims not to train on your data
sounds good on paper. For highly sensitive
applications, like handling health data, this is not
enough. Open-weight models can be self-
hosted, which gives the operator more control
over where inference data goes. It does not
guarantee that the whole application keeps no
leader when I started this experiment
Operating rooms have lots of equipment, and each
device brings its own controls. A voice assistant
could save you the constant reaching for knobs and
menus. But a natural command is not enough on its
own. The system has to identify which device and
setting the speaker means, handle values precisely,
and avoid changing anything the speaker did not ask
So let me quickly cook up a beautiful virtual room for
this experiment. This room has an

as gas flow, light brightness, table tilt, or endoscope

There are a lot of complex components involved to
make this work reliably in the real world. Luckily, the
virtual room simplifies things greatly and allows us
to focus on the narrow question of whether a
System-One model can turn short utterances into
actionable commands we can automatically apply to

modify the fields/attributes of the objects in the

System-One question types and example outputs.
For example, a question could ask which of several
light modes the speaker requested or what

model output is not the room state itself. Application
code still has to interpret the answer, apply limits,
and decide whether to act based on confidence
thresholds. The confidence score of a valid
is very important, as it cannot name an option
outside its criteria answer space, but it can still
choose an incorrect option. So that is our only way to
know how much to trust that confined answer.

running the model locally is important for GDPR
compliance. The less hardware is required, the easier
it is to set up for institutions, especially hospitals. So
naturally I wanted to try out how far we can get with
JevK5 has a model version with 2B parameters that
can somehow run on my RTX 2080. The server
exposes a System-One-compatible API, so the
surrounding request format stays close to the
hosted Jev example. I use the model and package

Overall metrics for Jev and JevK5-2B benchmark results.
In the recorded runs, Jev performs better than
JevK5-2B on utterance-level accuracy. Jev also
performs better in the rolling evaluation, where
predictions are applied through an utterance
sequence and earlier mistakes can affect later state.
I keep these measurements separate because
JevK5-2B has fewer evaluated cases. The paired
Overall metrics for Jev and JevK5-2B
uses the same cases for both
models and points in the same direction.

The table’s field macro-F1 averages per-field F1
scores, so a field with many examples does not
drown out one with poor performance. The models
do not have the same coverage in every sample set,
so treat this as a summary of the supplied
measurements rather than a like-for-like benchmark.

There may be a dataset issue here too. I discovered
cases where an utterance like “tilt table by 5
degrees” has an expected state of
which goes against my intuition and also against
per utterance. That is more than enough to count as

“It runs locally” and “it is useful locally” are
the local model ran on my RTX 2080, but this
particular 2B configuration was not fast enough
for the near-real-time interaction I had in mind.
System-One’s constrained outputs are an appealing
schema narrows what the model can return, and the
API scores each field directly. That is a much better
JevK5-2B did not turn out to be a practical local
substitute for Jev in this setup. It was less accurate
and much slower, and both models missed nearly
every positive safety-interlock case. If privacy is the
reason to run locally, it currently costs more
accuracy and latency than I would accept.
So no, local System-One control is not ready. But the
failure modes I saw could be explained by sub-
optimal data and instruction setup. Next steps are to
investigate whether better data and more guardrails
can close the gap without moving the safety
default checkpoint. I did not tune it, I just pointed
the server at it. My bet is that fine-tuning on
boundary cases and background noise buys more
than swapping architectures. That needs human-
reviewed labels instead of the generated ones I
used, which would also make the benchmark mean
more than “it works on my generated test set”.
The RTX 2080 is what I had, not what
I would buy for this. A newer card, or a smaller or
quantized checkpoint, would probably bring latency
into a comfortable range. Whether that gets below
the ~200 ms human response time on hardware a
hospital would actually buy, I have not tested.
validation and abstention on low confidence were
cheap to add, and they catch the errors the schema
lets through on its own. That being said, corrective
